lg.l: Informing [the confidante] about the type of separation,
[the hero] rightfully suffering when her companion speaks [of the heroine's state],

[the confidante] saying, “I know,” when there is no [more] anguish, [the confidante] speaking so that [the heroine] knows,This is not clear at all. Presumably it refers to the confidante informing the heroine about some aspect of his separation. There is no poem cited which clearly corresponds to this.
the one with the fragrant forehead lamenting, [the confidante] speaking so that [the heroine] becomes amenable [to the separation],
the one with the clear jewels agreeing, [the hero and his heart] becoming confused together during the journey,
[the heroine] suffering because the time [of his return] has come,

while the confidante says [the heroine] has suffered, [the hero] says she is one who [still] suffers,This is not clear. Based on the poems in the commentary, this situation includes lots of possible other situations. It is understood this way as this is how the author seems to have interpreted it, and there are no other sources of information.
and [the confidante] comforting [the heroine] — [let there be an understanding [that these situations] are the long-distance separation,
[which] also apply to the man who comes from 'that place'.

div.p: eṉpatu cēy iṭaip pirivām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which 'the long-distance separation' occurs.
pirivuṇarttutaṉ mutal ākap peyarntōṉ kūṟṟīṟākac collap paṭṭaṉa cēy iṭaip pirivām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with 'informing of the separation' and ending with the speech of the one who had returned, those things that have been mentioned are 'the long-distance separation'.

lg.l: I have firmly resolved to go away and bring wealth

as that will bringLiterally: “Because of the bringing of virtue... I have firmly resolved...” Exactly how to understand the listed items is unclear. Because of the syntax, the first three items are treated as one group, and then the final two as another which primarily concern their family. One could also translate: “bring virtue... and pleasure which our family will praise”. In this understanding, pukaḻum is a peyareccam rather than en element in the enumeration. The final option is that all the listed things are for the sake of their family. virtue, charity, love
and the praise and pleasure of all our family,
O you with the garland of open flowers and shining jewels.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ tōḻikkup pirivuṇarttiyatu.
The hero informs the confidante about his separation.

lg.l: What more shall I say, O loving man?
After you leftThis is a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam., her state of separationThis is referring to her state when he has separated from her.

where her breath leaves, alas, it appeared.This poem is a warning to him. A reminder about how the heroine reacted in the past when he went away just for short trips. One can read the poem slightly differently, where the the confidante is explicitly looking forward to what will happen without bringing up the past: “After you leave, her state... will appear.”

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṇilaimai kūṟic celavaḻuṅkuvittatu.
The confidante stopping [the hero] going by talking about the state of the heroine.

lg.l: I will say one thing, O lord.
If you desire an undertaking in the lonely distance,
where the clouds have dried up so the ground splits open,

will the pretty, dark young woman be able to bear that as well?The -um is not easy to understand. Perhaps it refers to another time he did something similar, or any other time her left her alone.naṭai is understood as 'a course of action' or 'way of doing things' here. It is not directly translated.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Even more so than her who had herself resolved to come

so that her suffering small feet wouldThis is not explicitly conveyed in the Tamil, but it is clear that the hero is talking about something that will happen if the comes in the future, and 'would' conveys that in English. become red on the way
and her colour would fade like a sprout that has left the branch,
my foolish heart, who rejoices [at going through]
the dense bamboo thickets with her, is very great.This final statement is ironic. Literally: “It possesses great worthiness.”

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉeñciṟkuc collic celavaḻuṅkuvittatu.
The hero desists from going after speaking to his heart.

lg.l: If one says, “a remedy?” [she is] a remedy
and if one says, “a treasure?” [she is] a treasure
— that good little daughter of the man from the rocky wilderness

with high-setpakaṭṭu can mean either 'high' or 'large'. Both are plausible attributes in this context. young breasts with groups of budding beauty spots,cuṇaṅku iṉam can be split differently as, cuṇaṅkiṉ am. In that case, the whole phrase would translate to: “pretty high-set/large breats with beauty spots”.
wide shoulders and a thin waist.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Once I have told her, as is correct,neṟi as 'the right course of action'. that this is what you intend,
know her stateHow she took the news, in other words. and then speak [to you],
you may unerringly yoke your horse to the tall gold-decorated chariot.

div.p: eṉpatu aḻuṅkātu celavu kuṟitta talaimakaṉukkut tōḻi colliyatu.
The confidante speaks to the hero who had inteded to go without restriction.

lg.l: I don't know, O friend, what his heart thinks.
Having become a man whose face grew pained
when the doe with a kid united with the stag,

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi talaimakaṭkuk kuṟippiṉāṟ pirivuṇarttiyatu.
The confidante indirectly informs the heroine of [the hero's] separation.

lg.l: Yearning for those people whose minds [know]
the moon-like Vedaskēḷvi can refer to either vedic knowledge, learning in general, or śruti, its Sanskrit calque. and explain things so the benefits

of the 18 compositions of limitless eruditionThis could refer to a number of things. The clearest options are: the patiṉeṇmēḻkaṉakku ('eighteen greater texts', i.e. the Caṅkam corpus), the patiṉeṇkīḻkaṉakku ('eighteen lesser texts', i.e. post-Caṅkam), or 18 languages as listed in the Naṉṉūl — ciṅkaḻam, cōṉakam, cāvakam, cīṉam, tuḷuvam, kuṭakam, koṅkaṇam, kaṉṉaṭam, kollam, teluṅku, kaliṅkam, vaṅkam, kaṅkam, makatam, kaṭāram, kavuṭam, kōcalam, tamiḻ. are obtained,
our lover will set off and separate for other lands.

div.p: eṉpatu kalvi viḷakkuvāṉ pirivar eṉa veḷip paṭa vuṇarttiyatu.
[The confidante] informs [the heroine] clearly that he will separate for the sake of further study.

lg.l: It is the duty of the young woman with beautiful jewels
to support [her] lover who desiresOr, 'who needs to', 'who is wanted for', 'who is needed for'. the guard
that protects life on the great vast world.

div.p: eṉpatu kāttaṟkup pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
[The confidante] informs [the heroine] that he will separate to guard [the realm].

lg.l: Our beloved will leave for his manly undertaking
where he will remove the thicket of fighting spearsThis is a common way to express a melee. Cf. Pati12.1, 31.20, 33.7 for some examples.

for the two great kings of undiminished victory.mīḷā veṉṟi is not clear. I have understood it as a vicotry (veṉṟi) which does not disappear (mīḷā), i.e an ever-present or undiminshed victory. There is another meaning for mīḷ-tal, common in the kiḷavi-s - 'to return'. It is possible to translate with this meaning. One could argue that the word-order was distorted for the sake of etukai, though that is not a common feature of this collection of poems. In that case: "two great kings who will not return victorous", where the implication would be that if the hero did not intervene, the result would be bad for both the great kings. Alternatively, one can translate: “two kings for whom victory has not returned”. Indeed one can see that the phrase has been understood both ways in the past. In his 1939 translation of the Cilappatikāram, Ramachandra Dikshitar translates the phrase mīḷā veṉṟi in 13:143 as, " who would not return from the field victorious" (Ramachandra Dikshitar 1939: 196; in this translation he understands a different headword for mīḷā veṉṟi, not given in the quotation) and then as, "the monarch of unfailing success" (Ramachandra Dikshitar 1939: 293). These are the only two times the phrase occurs in the old corpus, to the best of my knowledge. The chosen translation retains word order and makes sense in the context of two great kings going to battle. Additionaly Aṭiyārkkunallār glosses the phrase with, maṭaṅkāta veṉṟiyaiyuṭaiya vēntaṉ ('the king who possesses unbending/unsurrendering victory') in his commentary to 13:143. It was suggested to me by Dr. Indra Manuel that this may refer to a type of battle called tumpaittiṇai from puṟapporuḷ, a "Major theme of a king or warrior heroically fighting against his enemy" (TL).

div.p: eṉpatu pakai taṇippāṉ pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
[The confidante] informs [the heroine] that he will separate to appease enmity.

lg.l: Of course [your] lover will go because of the enmitypakai micai is understood in this translation as a loctive that has some of the force of 'for the sake of', or 'on account of'. Another option would be to translate: “[your] lover will go to the enemies of the king.” Here pakai is understood as 'enemies'.
towards the king with the great army, won't he?
O, stop your suffering, one with the white lotus garland!

div.p: eṉpatu vēntaṟ kuṟṟuḻip pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
[The confidante] informs [the heroine] that he will separate for a royal emergency.

lg.l: Our lover left for shining wealth thinking,
"There is no praise at all for those men who delight in sitting at home
while abstaining from manly work day after day."

div.p: eṉpatu poruḷ vayiṟ pirivar eṉa vuṇarttiyatu.
[The confidante] informs [the heroine] that he will separate for the sake of wealth.

lg.l: If it is said that he will not go, please say!
If [you] say he has changed [his mind] and is quickly returning,Lit., “If [you] say [there is] the returning of him who changed”.

there is no problem. Speak for the man who lives this way!There is another way to construe this if one understands iṉṟu as 'without', instead of as a finite verb: “If [you] speak about the quick return of the man who changed [his mind/course], speak for the man who lives this way without obstacles!”

div.p: eṉpatu pirivar eṉpatu kēṭṭa talaimakaḷ āṟṟāḷ āyt tōḻikkuc colliyatu.
The heroine, who had heard that he will separate, cannot bear it and speaks to the confidante.

lg.l: Who can separate while you, eyes overflowing with water, remain here?
[There will be] going with you with a bright forehead swarmed by bees,
because of the honey scent which smells of
the pretty summer branches of the twisting, windingvalam can also mean 'might', in which case this could refer to a tree this is very windy. Marām tree,
which the mountainside slopes take as an adornment.

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ āya talaimakaṭkut tōḻi pirivu nayappac colliyatu.
The confidante speaks to the heroine, who had become unable to bear [the situation], to make her agree to the separation.

lg.l: Desiring the creation of good fame,
separating from his mate and going is the duty of the lover.
Sitting at home and bearing [this] without anger
with a dignifiedōṅkiya literally means 'to be high'. One can think of this as an equivalent to 'high-class' when it describes someone's charater. heart is the nature of married life.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: The man from the land with the high mountains with flowing waterfalls,
— as though one is looking like the moon rise over the sea,
he is like the sun, O friend —
and my large bamboo arms are like the Neruñci plant.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ pirivuṭaṉ paṭṭatu.
The heroine agrees to [the hero's] separation.

lg.l: Thinking of the crossroads in the difficult desert
and of the very cool northern wind which will come

because you separated,This causal construction has been translated faithfully, but perhaps 'when' might be more apt than 'because'. It is not clear whether the idea is that the wind actually comes because he has left, whether it is painful because he has left, or simply that this will occur once he has left. we shall suffer.

div.p: eṉpatu pirivuṭaṉ paṭṭa talaimakaṭalaimakaṟkuc colliyatu.
The heroine, who had agreed to [his] separation, speaks to the hero.

lg.l: Now we have impelled the horsesOne can either understand kaṭum pari as a metonymic reference to the horses, as in the translation, or as literally: “Now we have driven the tall chariot at a great speed”. of the tall chariot
whose nature is like the wind, gone to the wilderness of Pālai trees
and completed our work, let us return!
The loneliness of the girl with a body like gold is very great.

div.p: eṉpatu pirintu cellun talaimakaṉ ṟērp pākaṟkuc colliyatu.
The hero, who had separated [from the heroine] and left, speaks to the charioteer.

lg.l: You did not stay [with her] there in that place.
Now rise here in this place! Live, my heart!
Becauseporuḷ vayiṉāṉ is more literally, “for the sake of the wealth...”. we have resolved on making wealth,

the dark kajal eyes of the girl of humble words weep.The syntax of the last two and a half lines can be construed differently. As understood in the translation, they are a standalone phrase which relates condition for the state of the heroine, but there is no finite verb. The other options would be to either connect poruḷ vayiṉāṉ to the root imperative in which which case the poem would read, “rise here, for the sake of the wealth...”, or as a kind of predicate for īṇṭi ivaṇ and understand vayiṉāṉ literally instead of as a locative posposition. This would translate to: “Rise here, in this way, in the place of the wealth [we] resolved to make...”.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ iṭaic curattut talaimakaḷai niṉaintu neñciṉait teḷittuc ceṉṟatu.
The hero, after clarifying [the matter] with his heart, who was thinking of the heroine in the middle of the desert, goes on.

lg.l: I was careless thinking, “He won't go.”

And he stayed behindoḻintaṉar can also be understood as 'he left aside' or 'he declined'. In that case the line would read: “he declined [to invite me] saying...”. In both cases the hero does not ask the heroine to join him on his journey thinking she will refuse. Whether or not he has actually left for his trip at the time when this is spoken is not clear. It is also not clear in KT43, though in PK300 he has left. thinking, “She won't agree.”
O one with the good beautiful kajal eyes,

my heart wastes away.Presumably this means that he has now left, having previously stayed without inviting her, but this is not certain.This final phrase could also br translated: “My heart, my good beautiful kajal eyes are wasting away.”

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ aṟiyāmaṟ pirinta viṭattut talaimakaḷ āṟṟātu colliyatu.
Without knowledge of the hero during the separation, the heroine speaks, unable to bear it.

lg.l: They are foolish: as the Malabar glory-lily appears,
having joined with the Piṭavu and Kōṭal
along with the laburnum which makes garlands,
the forest understands [it is]One can understand koṇṭaṉṟu differently as 'to take on [the appearance]'. the rainy season.

O, our eyes do indeed take on water.The speech situation is not clear. If the speaker has already stated the flowers are foolish, then why have they become disconsolate? Perhaps one out to understand maṭava as an unmarked instrumental: “Because they are foolish, as they appeared, the forest took [the appearance of] the rainy season”. Then the final line is a comparison to the flowers — an implicit statement that their tears are also foolish.

div.p: eṉpatu paruvavaravu kaṇṭāṟṟāḷ āyatu.
On seeing the season [of his arrival] coming, [the heroine] becomes disconsolate.

lg.l: Live, O friend! Has our life forgotten [us]Could there be another subject for this verb? If one supplies one like 'my/our beauty', then the comparison in the poem is more elegant: “Has [my beauty] forgotton our life [together] like him? Because he has separated... so has my beauty.” like him?
Since the man from the land with forests,
where parakeets are chased away from the millet
by the beating of pestles in the houses, left,
my dark beauty — it also left.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Small bleak evening! Small bleak evening!
After the cool wind blows like a fiery chill,
and you take away the redness,Another way to express the sun setting.

small bleak evening,The peyareccam phrase ... koṇṭa ciṟu puṉ mālai is not accurately rendered as the main poetic play here is the repetition of the phrase ciṟu puṉ mālai, and this was the most close and natural way to retain that. you come to us daily.
You never go to his hilly land!

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmaikkut tōḻi yāṟṟāḷ āyiṟṟu.
The confidante, because the heroine cannot bear [the separation], becomes disconsolate.

lg.l: They say it is not pleasing, that difficult desert,
where the stomachs grow pained of the mothers of the young men
commanded by the taṇṇumaiA type of war drum. drum being suitably beaten

by the pulaiyaṉ to say, “You men in a line, go!”This type of imperative ending in -mō normally has a polite nuance — 'please go'. This phrase is alluding to some kind of war formation, so this may be because the appropriate form of address from their own general.
What of the road he travels, O friend?

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ āya tōḻikkāṟṟuval eṉpatu paṭac colliyatu.
[The heroine] speaks to the confidante, who had become disconsolate, to be told something comforting.

lg.l: So that, as scandal and great blame spread, [our] goodness was ruined

and pallor spread on [our] suffering small foreheads -The two infinitve clauses can both be understood and co-ordinated temporal clauses, so: "While... spread, and while [our] goodness... spread". Alternatively, they can both be understood as reultative: "So that... spread, and so that [our] goodness... spread". The chosen translation does not require co-ordination.
are the hills in his land even crueler
than that man who did this to us? O friend,

not even one [cloud] has appearedtōṉṟā is a polysemous form. It can either be analysed as a negative absolutive, as done in the translation; as a negative neuter plural; or as a contracted form of the negative neuter singular. ALl of the options result in a similar meaning of the poem - no rain clouds appear - but the finite forms require two clauses in the final sentence in the translation to be split into two finite sentences. and the rains have failed.In the phrase, maḻai maṟantaṉa, both words can be translated differently: maḻai as either 'rain' or 'cloud', and maṟa-ttal as either 'to forget' or 'to fail'. In AN 241.7 and Tēv. 7:55.2, almost the same phrase refers to the rains failing, so I have followed that here, though either 'clouds' or 'rain' would refer to the same thing - the rainy season. Seeing as the point of comparison in the poem is between the cruelty of the hero and cruelty of the hills, taking maṟa-ttal as 'to fail' is more sensible. Then, the hills cruelly prevent the rain clouds from reaching the heroine, along with the hero, who had promised to return before the rains. If one takes the verb as 'to forget', the cruelty of the clouds, not of the hills which is emphasised.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi yāṟṟuvippāṉ ṟalaimakaṉai iyaṟ paḻittatu.
The confidante belittles the nature of the hero to comfort [the heroine].

lg.l: Although [my] arms speak of his cruelty by becoming emaciated
so that the bangles slip and fall down,Lit., “walk and fall down”. there is no cruelty
on the part of the man from the land with good mountains, O friend.
He has not separated from my heart and,

with a single glance to his hill,This could work two ways. Either the final two lines enforce the fact that the heroine bears no ill will towards the hero, or they can work as a final lament. For the first situation, see the translation presented, for the second: “He does not chase away [my distress] with the sight of his hill.” i.e. nothing can cure my pain apart from his return. The reading from the TKn, tam kuṟai, to which Dr. Indra Manuel suggested emending, works nicely: “and he does not discard his pleading look”. In this case, the poem is the heroine justifying the hero's behaviour by saying she still knows he loves her. In line with the philosophy of this edition, the MS reading is retained. he is without [my] disapproval.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ ataṉukkāṟṟāḷ āy moḻintatu.
The heroine, having become disconsolate on account of that [separation], speaks.

lg.l: Even more than her who suffers, thinking, “This is the rainy season.”

because the dark clouds full of water had weakened and issued forth their burden,How to take uruttal is not totally clear. The emendation by UVC makes good sense — for the rain cloud to shed their burden — but the poem is still understandable without it. As similar meaning meaning is arrived at in the translation presented. Another option would be to take uruttal in its meaning of 'to mature', in which case: “the clouds full of water weakened and matured [with regards to] their burden [of rain]”.
after not understanding and seeing the new cool rains,Cf. KT382.4 for vampu referring to a specific type of rain left over from the previous rainy season.
all the great cool Jasmine, which budded in open clusters of buds,
like the teeth of the brilliant smile on her mouth,
deserveLit., “possess the suitability for...”. to be laughed at.

div.p: eṉpatu paruvam aṉṟeṉa vāṟṟuvittatu.
[The confidante] comforts [the heroine] by saying, “It is not the season [of his return].”

lg.l: Even though you think ofThis must carry some sort of negative connotation for the concessive to make sense. The reference to the 'long way' may suggest the heroine is think primarily of the difficulty and danger of the road. the long way
where pollen sits atop the Kōpam cactus,
and the heavy rain in the forest, made by the rainy season itself,The -ē on kār-ē is a bit ambiguous. Is this to state that the forest only exists thanks to the rainy season?

the chariot of that most worthy manneṭum takai is understood as a synonym of perum takai. One can find it used as such a number of time in the PN (cf.PN272.7 and 296.5, for example). One could also take both neṭum and takai as as properties of the chariot, in which case: “the tall, worthy chariot has come so that...”. has come
so that hearts rejoice and the birds rise up.

div.p: eṉpatu tēr varavu kūṟi yāṟṟuvittatu.
[The confidante] comforting [the heroine] by talking about [the hero's] chariot coming.

lg.l: In the confusing dark evening, whenever [she] hears
the sorrowful āmpal fluteThis could also be the name of a specific melody, and presumably has some sort of romantic connotation. of the many cowherds
amongst the Jasmine in the clearings between the crowded houses
does the pitiful one, our beloved, become agitated?

div.p: eṉpatu viṉai muṭittu mīḷvāṉeñciṟkuc colliyatu.
Having completed his task, the one who was returning speaks to his heart.

lg.l: O great cloud full of rain, stop your cruelOr 'quick' journey,
as the girl with eyes overflowing with tears
will become lonely, thinking her lover won't return.Lit., “has become one has not returned”.

div.p: eṉpatu mukilukkuc colliyatu.
[The hero] speaks to a cloud.

lg.l: Please mount the chariot, O charioteer!
we must go there nowippoḻuti aḷavaiyiṉ pukuka nām literally translates to: “We must go there within this measure of time!” I.e. “We must go there now!”. to see the girl who,

on seeing the rains,A similar idea is expressed in PK259, cited for the poem above, where the hero wants to arrive home before the rainy season. will keeppulantu uṟaivōḷ can also mean: “who conducts herself worriedly”, or “being worried about us, she is one who is at home...” worrying about us thinking,

div.p: eṉpatu tērp pākaṟkuc colliyatu.
[The hero] speaks to the charioteer.

lg.l: Because you revealed the coming of the lover,
may you live long onuḻai here function as a locative postposition. this world with a blooming expanse,

O moon[-like conch]The moon here is a metaphor for the conch. Its curling rays give away that this is the case. A common attribute of a conch is that it is rightward-spiralling — pulantu uṟaivōḷ. Cf. PN225.12, 283.7. UVC emends to conch, but that is not necessary. with a face around which rays wind.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi caṅkiṉai vāḻttiyatu.
The confidante praises the conch.
eṉpatu talaimakaṭkut tōḻi colliyatu.
The confidante speaks to the heroine.

lg.l: But for [my] body which remained there with difficulty,
would my heart which had been united with your innocent glance
have been able to bear separation from you?

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṭkut talaimakaṉ colliyatu. 24.
The hero speaks to the heroine.

standOff.note: Cf. TP25n: ōtal pakaiyē tūtivai pirivē ||
Cf. IA45: pukaḻum koṭumaiyum kiḻavōṉ mēṉa

Both C1 and Cām. mean the same - they are neuter singular obliques of the root uri- ('to have the right'), used abverbially. uritiṉiṉ clearly became the standard form after a point, but there is not grammatical reason is discount uritaṉiṉ. There are other examples of this variant (see AN 186.17: uritiṉiṉ in Irākavaiyaṅkār's 1923 edition; uritaṉiṉ in Wilden's upcoming edition, currently only published online without an apparatus, found at ), including another in this text (TNV18, poem 7), also emended to uritiṉiṉ by UVC. My impression is that such variants were normalised in the majority of cases. As it is a perfectly valid form transmitted by C1 and it is documented elsewhere, I retain the 'variant' form.

The pattern in this cūttiram is clear: each situation enumertated ends in a verbal noun finishing in -al. There is not direct parallel I ahve found for this phrase or for this situation in another grammatical treatise or koḷu/kiḷavi, so I assume UVC emended here for that reason. This pattern, however, is not a constant through the rest of the TNV. There are multiple cūṭtiram-s which use different syntactic constructions to describe situations. In TNV 20, for example, all but the final sitaution in the enumeration end in a verbal noun in -al. The final ends in the noun kiḷavi, a synonym for kūṟṟu in this this context. One sees it used in a similar context in the second layer of the commentary: peyarntōṉ kūṟṟu ('the speech of the one who returned'). Since the reading in Cām. seems to be pure conjecture and there is some evidence that it is unneccessary, the reading is maintained. The remaining doubt I have is that kūṟṟu is always preceded by an agent in the TNV (and somewhat curiously, it only appears from TNV 23 onwards and then with some regularity, though I do not think this is meaningful). One can construe the phrase with nōvāḷ as the agent, though there are other possiblities (see the translation notes on the opposite page). Even if one interprets it differently, I would argue the C1 reading reading is still perfectly comprehensible, though it becomes less convincing.

Both varal and varavu are nominal derivations from vā-/varu-tal and neither are particularly common directly preceding a verbs of speech like we find in this poem ('tell about his coming'). In general, I do not see a clear syntactic pattern where the object of description ought to be the nominal derivation ending in -vu as opposed to in -al. varavu uraittal is a phrase ofund in the koḷu-s to the TK and PPVM (see TK156 and PPVM2.14, for example), which may have convinced UVC to emend. There is one text-internal example of a nominal derivation in -vu preceding uraittal, in TNV 20.1: ayal varaviu uraittal ('[the confidante] talking about marriage [offers from] the neighbourhood'). I am not convinced that this is meaningful. Due to the structure of the cūttiram, where verbal nouns ending in -al end a speech-situation, the author might not have wanted to use one apart from in that function, to save confusion. There is, however, some evidence in support of C1 from the Caṅkam corpus. In some editions of the AN, and one documented manuscript, poem 35.15 reads: iṉṟu varal uraimō ('tell [me] of [his] coming today'; Irākavaiyaṅkār 1923). It seems this was a valid and recorded construction, so since it is reported by C1, I retain it.
One does not expect any consontant gemination after an enclitic ē.

The C2, KT etc. reading makes perfect sense — the -um on niṉṉoṭum is co-ordinating with the hero, i.e. the two of them going together. This is not, however, necessary, so this edition retains the C1 reading. Probably incedentally, the same phrase, as found in C1, appears as the final two cīr-s in PN 265.
This poem is addressed to the heroine, according to the koḷu, so C1's reading does not make sense. It would require this to be addressed to the hero, as kātala is a vocative.

Both readings are perfectly sensible, and neither have clear parallels in a prior text, so I am not sure why UVC emended. Perhaps he thought it was more appropriate for the heroine to sit at home with a sad, weakened heart (ōṅkiya uḷḷam), though it seems equally plausible in the context of the poem that she ought to feel a sense of dignity and even pride - her husband is doing himself (and by extension, her) proud, and she is performing her duty.

In terms of meaning, there is little difference between C1pc and C2 on. I preserve C1pc not because I argue it is the 'original' reading, but to retain evidence of what I believe is a strand of transmission. It is not clear why UVC chose to emend here. C1 makes good sense (to me, at least). paṉippu is the abstract noun of the strong root paṉi-ttal 'to become cold', so 'a chill' in this context, or something similar. This works perfectly well as a comparison. Reading paṉi ('dew', 'coldness') reads well, but I question the necessity of deviating from the manusctipt. There are no parallels for this phrase I have found, and the TPn reading agrees with C1.

nalaṉ aḻintu and nalaṉ iḻantu both make sense and produce a similar meaning: either the heroine's goodness is ruined, as in C1, or lost in the case of Cām. There is one Caṅkam parral I have found for C1 in Kali 134.7, but many for the Cām. reading. It is perfectly possible that both C1 and TPn are the result of a similar scribal error, but unlikely that the two would independently arrive at the same uncommon, but sensible, collocation, so I retain C1's reading.

There is very little difference in meaning here between C1 and Cām. etc, but Cām.'s reading makes for a cleaner syntax. The ummai particle in C1 - kuṉṟu-um - is slightly awkward. If one takes it as a kind of eccavummai, then it is a bit redundant with the comparative avariṉum. Its distributive function makes more sense - "all of the hills" - but it is still unnecessary. We also find kuṉṟam in the final line of the next poem. I think here there is enough reason to move away from a grammatically inelegant MS reading, which is also supported by TPn. There are no reported varaints in any edition of the TPn which I have found.

Unlike in the above case, I think a strong argument can be made against TPn. maḻai maṟa-ttal ('rain/clouds failed [to come]') has parallels in AN241.7, where the heorine complains of the rains failing when her lover is away, and Tēv. 7:55.2. maḻai maṟai-tal has only one Caṅkam quasi-parallel I have found in AiN 252.2, where clouds hide huts. There, one finds maṟai-ttal, the transitive form. If one were to take Cām.'s reading, it could be understood two ways: either where the hills or the clouds are the subject if maṟai-tal ('to be hidden'). If the clouds, then the general sense of the poem remains the same - the rain clouds are hidden by the cruel clouds. If the hills are the subject, then they are hidden behind the clouds, and the heroine is unable to remind herself of her lover with their sight. We see this idea in the next poem, but it seems unlikely here as it would give agency to the clouds, where the comparison in the poem is between the hills and the hero.
